question: What is the purpose of @BeforeEach and @AfterEach in JUnit 5?
title: @BeforeEach @AfterEach JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@BeforeEach`** runs before *every* test method and **`@AfterEach`** runs after every test method. Their job is **test isolation**: rebuild fresh state before each test and release resources after, so tests never leak data into one another. Because JUnit creates a new test instance per method, this combined with `@BeforeEach` guarantees each test starts clean.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand these run per-test (not once) and why that enforces test independence
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing @BeforeEach with @BeforeAll, or relying on field state set up in a previous test instead of @BeforeEach
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie @BeforeEach to the FIRST 'Independent' principle and the fresh-instance-per-test model

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@BeforeEach`** runs before every test; **`@AfterEach`** after every test.
- **Isolation** — fresh state per test enforces FIRST 'Independent'.
- **Fresh instance** — JUnit creates a new test object per method.
- **`@AfterEach` runs on failure** — the safe place for cleanup.
- **Not `@BeforeAll`** — that runs once and is static.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
BeforeEach and AfterEach are lifecycle hooks that run around every single test method. BeforeEach runs right before each test, and AfterEach runs right after. The whole point of them is test isolation. I use BeforeEach to build fresh objects so each test starts from a clean, known state, and I use AfterEach to release resources like files or connections.

This ties into how JUnit works under the hood. By default, JUnit creates a brand new instance of the test class for each test method. That's a deliberate design choice to keep tests independent. BeforeEach complements that by rebuilding the state, so no test can accidentally depend on data another test left behind. For example, if I'm testing a shopping cart, my BeforeEach creates a new empty cart before each test, so the test that adds an item isn't polluted by a previous test.

A really important detail is that AfterEach runs even if the test fails. That makes it the safe place for cleanup — if I did cleanup at the end of the test body and the test failed partway through, the resource would leak.

The common mistake is confusing BeforeEach with BeforeAll. BeforeEach runs before every test, while BeforeAll runs just once for the whole class and has to be static. Putting expensive setup in BeforeEach slows everything down, but putting shared mutable state in BeforeAll breaks isolation. To stand out, I'd connect this to the Independent principle in FIRST — fresh state per test is exactly what keeps tests from interfering with each other.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**`@ExtendWith`** registers a JUnit 5 **extension** — a plugin that hooks into the test lifecycle.

The common ones are **`MockitoExtension`** (enables `@Mock`/`@InjectMocks` and verifies stubbing) and **`SpringExtension`** (loads the Spring context).

It replaces JUnit 4's `@RunWith`, and crucially you can apply **several extensions** to one class, whereas `@RunWith` allowed only a single runner.

A common mistake is confusing @BeforeEach with @BeforeAll, or relying on field state set up in a previous test instead of @BeforeEach

sections.title: Per-Test Lifecycle
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["new test instance"] --> B["@BeforeEach
build fresh state"] B --> C["@Test
run one test"] C --> D["@AfterEach
clean up resources"] D --> E["repeat for
next test"] ```

sections.title: Fresh State Before Each Test
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing Each with All.** `@BeforeEach` runs per test; `@BeforeAll` runs once. Heavy setup in `@BeforeEach` slows the suite, but shared mutable setup in `@BeforeAll` breaks isolation.
- **Relying on leftover state.** Expecting a field populated by a previous test — fragile and order-dependent. Build state in `@BeforeEach`.
- **Cleanup in the test body.** If the test fails before cleanup, resources leak. Put cleanup in `@AfterEach`.
- **Using JUnit 4 names.** It's `@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach`, not `@Before`/`@After`.

question: What does @DisplayName do in JUnit 5 and why should you use it?
title: @DisplayName JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@DisplayName`** gives a test method or class a **human-readable name** shown in IDEs, Maven Surefire reports, and CI dashboards instead of the raw method name. It can contain spaces, punctuation, even emoji, so reports read like specifications — `@DisplayName("rejects withdrawal above balance")`. It's documentation that doesn't change behavior.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you value readable test reports and know @DisplayName is purely for reporting
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking @DisplayName replaces good method names, or that it affects test discovery/execution
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Pair @DisplayName with @Nested so reports read as full sentences; keep method names descriptive too

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@DisplayName`** = free-form readable label for a test or class.
- **Shows** in IDEs, Surefire reports, and CI dashboards.
- **No behavior change** — purely cosmetic.
- **Pairs with `@Nested`** so reports read as full sentences.
- **Keep method names good too** — code readers don't see display names.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
DisplayName gives a test or a test class a human-readable name that shows up in the IDE, in the Maven Surefire report, and on CI dashboards, instead of the raw Java method name. Method names have to follow Java identifier rules, so they end up camel-cased and a bit awkward to read. A display name is just a free-form string, so it can have spaces and punctuation. That means a report can say rejects a withdrawal larger than the balance, which reads like a specification, instead of the squished method name.

The key thing to understand is that it's purely cosmetic. It doesn't affect which tests are discovered, the order they run in, or whether they run at all — it only changes the label in reports. So it's really a documentation feature.

Where it shines is combined with the Nested annotation. If I have a nested class with a display name and tests with display names, the report reads as a full sentence — something like BankAccount, when empty, rejects a withdrawal. That's genuinely useful when a non-engineer, like a QA lead or a product owner, is looking at the CI output.

The mistakes I'd avoid are letting the method names get sloppy because I'm relying on display names — teammates still read the method names in the source — and writing vague display names like test one, which throws away the benefit. To stand out, I'd mention pairing DisplayName with Nested to produce business-readable reports while still keeping the method names descriptive for whoever reads the code.

question: What is @ExtendWith in JUnit 5 and when do you use it?
title: @ExtendWith JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@ExtendWith`** registers a JUnit 5 **extension** — a plugin that hooks into the test lifecycle. The common ones are **`MockitoExtension`** (enables `@Mock`/`@InjectMocks` and verifies stubbing) and **`SpringExtension`** (loads the Spring context). It replaces JUnit 4's `@RunWith`, and crucially you can apply **several extensions** to one class, whereas `@RunWith` allowed only a single runner.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know extensions are how JUnit 5 integrates with Mockito/Spring and that you can stack them
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Still using @RunWith with JUnit 5, or forgetting @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) so @Mock fields stay null
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the extension model is composable and SpringExtension is already inside @SpringBootTest/@WebMvcTest

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@ExtendWith`** registers a lifecycle extension (plugin).
- **`MockitoExtension`** enables `@Mock`/`@InjectMocks`.
- **`SpringExtension`** loads the Spring context.
- **Replaces `@RunWith`** and is **composable** (stack several).
- **Already bundled** inside `@SpringBootTest` and friends.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
ExtendWith is how I register an extension in JUnit 5, and an extension is basically a plugin that hooks into the test lifecycle. It can run code before and after tests, resolve parameters, or post-process the test instance. I just point ExtendWith at the extension class and JUnit wires it in.

The two I use all the time are the Mockito extension and the Spring extension. The Mockito extension initializes my Mock and InjectMocks fields and also reports unnecessary stubbing, which catches mistakes. The Spring extension boots up the Spring application context so I can autowire beans in a test.

The history here matters. In JUnit 4 you used RunWith, and the big limitation was that you could only have one runner per class. So you had to choose between, say, the Mockito runner and the Spring runner. JUnit 5 replaced that with the extension model, and the key improvement is that it's composable — I can stack multiple extensions on the same class. That's a real practical win.

The most common fresher mistake is still using RunWith with JUnit 5, in which case it's just ignored and your Mock fields come back null, so you get a NullPointerException on the first stub. The fix is ExtendWith with the Mockito extension. Another subtle point is that you don't add the Spring extension manually when you're already using SpringBootTest or WebMvcTest, because those meta-annotations already include it. To stand out, I'd emphasize that the extension model is composable and that SpringExtension is baked into the Spring Boot test slices.

sections.title: JUnit 4: a single @RunWith runner
JUnit 5: @ExtendWith, stackable
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `@RunWith` in JUnit 5.** It's ignored; `@Mock` fields stay null. Use `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`.
- **Forgetting the extension entirely.** No extension means no mock initialization — NPE at the first stub.
- **Re-adding SpringExtension.** `@SpringBootTest`, `@WebMvcTest`, and `@DataJpaTest` already include it; don't add it twice.
- **Mixing Mockito init styles.** Pick the extension or `MockitoAnnotations.openMocks` — not both.

question: What is @Nested in JUnit 5 and how does it improve test organization?
title: @Nested Tests JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@Nested`** groups related tests in an **inner, non-static class** so the report reads like an outline — grouping a unit's tests by state or scenario (e.g. `WhenEmpty`, `WhenFunded`). Outer `@BeforeEach` runs before the nested class's `@BeforeEach`, letting you layer setup from general to specific. It improves readability and makes failures self-locating.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can structure a large test class by scenario and understand nested setup ordering
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Making the nested class static, over-nesting, or grouping unrelated units together
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain layered @BeforeEach ordering and pairing @Nested with @DisplayName for sentence-like reports

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Nested`** = inner non-static class grouping a scenario.
- **Layered setup** — outer `@BeforeEach` before inner `@BeforeEach`.
- **Non-static required** — static breaks it.
- **Pair with `@DisplayName`** for sentence-like reports.
- **Same unit only** — split unrelated units into separate classes.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Nested is an annotation I put on an inner, non-static class to group related tests, and it really improves how a big test class reads. Without it, you get a flat list of test methods. With it, the report turns into an outline — for a bank account I might have a group called when empty and another called when funded with a hundred, and the relevant tests sit inside each group. So when something fails, the report tells me the scenario right away.

The part that makes it powerful is the layered setup. Each nested class can have its own BeforeEach, and JUnit runs the outer BeforeEach first and then the inner one. So the outer BeforeEach creates a fresh account, and inside the funded group the inner BeforeEach deposits a hundred. That lets me build context from general to specific instead of repeating setup in every test.

There are a couple of gotchas. The nested class has to be non-static, because it needs access to the outer instance — if I make it static, JUnit won't pick it up as a nested test class. And if I want a BeforeAll inside a nested class, I have to switch to the per-class lifecycle, since BeforeAll is normally static. I also try not to nest more than about two levels deep.

The rule of thumb is to use Nested to group the same unit's tests by state or condition, and to keep genuinely different units in separate top-level classes. To stand out, I'd mention the outer-then-inner BeforeEach ordering and pairing Nested with DisplayName so the reports read like full sentences.

sections.title: Scenario Grouping with Layered Setup
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Static nested class.** `@Nested` requires non-static so it can access the outer instance; `static` breaks discovery.
- **`@BeforeAll` inside a nested class.** Needs `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` since `@BeforeAll` is static by default.
- **Over-nesting.** Three-plus levels hurt readability; two is usually enough.
- **Grouping unrelated units.** Different classes under test belong in separate top-level test classes.
